docs.title: Home
docs.text:
RAGmen

Noodles are nodes. Instant GraphRAG without the long cooking.

  • Turn documents into a knowledge graph

    Feed RAGmen your PDFs, markdown files, or text documents and it builds a structured map of facts and relationships — not just a pile of chunks.

  • Ask questions. Get cited answers.

    Every answer comes with the exact source and page number. The AI stays strictly within your documents and never invents information.

  • Multi-source, conflict-aware

    When two documents disagree, RAGmen surfaces both versions with attribution instead of silently picking one.

  • Resumable, incremental, content-addressed

    Re-adding an unchanged file costs nothing. Interrupted runs resume where they stopped. Only changed sections are re-extracted.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["📄 Your documents\nPDF / MD / TXT"] --> B

    subgraph B["① Blueprint — Design once"]
        B1["Define what\nto look for"]
        B2["Approve\nthe schema"]
        B1 --> B2
    end

    B --> C

    subgraph C["② Forge — Build once per source"]
        C1["Chunk"] --> C2["Extract"] --> C3["Resolve"] --> C4["Embed"] --> C5["Write"]
    end

    C --> D[("Neo4j\nKnowledge Graph")]

    D --> E

    subgraph E["③ Serve — Per question"]
        E1["Vector search\n+ Keyword\n+ Graph traversal"]
    end

    E --> F["💬 Cited answers\nwith source + page"]

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
1. Install2. Start the database3. Add a document4. Build the graph5. Ask a question 
git clone https://github.com/Kamaal404/RAGmen.git
cd RAGmen
cd forge && pip install -e ".[dev]" && cd ..
cd serve && pip install -e ".[dev]" && cd ..
cd agent && pip install -e ".[dev]" && cd ..

docker compose up -d

forge add manual.pdf --blueprint spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml

forge cook src-abc123

lattice-serve --store neo4j --blueprint spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml &
agent ask "how do I build a dakota fire hole?"

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
forge: command not found

The forge package was not installed, or the wrong Python environment is active.

cd forge && pip install -e ".[dev]"

Verify: forge --help

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'forge'

Same root cause. If using a virtual environment (venv, conda), make sure it is activated before installing and running.

pip: command not found

Try: python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Connection refused: bolt://localhost:7687

Neo4j is not running.

docker compose up -d

Wait ~10 seconds, then retry. Verify Docker is open and running:

docker ps
Authentication failure on Neo4j

The credentials in .env do not match what Neo4j was initialized with.

Check your .env:

NEO4J_USER=neo4j
NEO4J_PASSWORD=password

These must match the values in docker-compose.yml. If you changed the password in the Neo4j browser, update .env to match.

Database is empty after forge cook

Three possible causes:

  1. forge cook used --store memory — in-memory data disappears when the command exits. Run again with --store neo4j.

  2. Indexes not created — run make reset to wipe and restart the database, then run forge cook again.

  3. Run was interrupted — run forge cook src-abc123 again, it will resume from the last completed chunk.

docs.title: Blueprint
docs.text:
blueprint is invalid: pattern source unknown

A pattern references a node type not declared in node_types.

Example: 

pattern [Ingredient, USED_IN, Recipe] — source label 'Ingredient' not in node_types

Fix: either add Ingredient to node_types, or correct the pattern.

blueprint is invalid: invalid regex

A hierarchy or skip_regions pattern is not valid Python regex.

Test your regex at regex101.com (Python flavor). In YAML, backslashes need escaping: use \\d+ not \d+.

blueprint not approved

You tried to run forge add with an unapproved blueprint.

Fix: once satisfied with the blueprint, add:

approved: true
approved_by: your-name
approved_at: "2026-10-12"

docs.title: Extraction
docs.text:
openai API key not set

Add your key to .env:

OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

For testing without an API key:

forge extract src-abc123 --provider mock
Extraction is very slow

Normal rate: 1–3 chunks per second. A 300-page book (~150 chunks) takes 2–5 minutes.

If stuck for >20 minutes: - Check your API key has not hit a rate limit or quota - Press Ctrl+C to stop, then run forge cook again — it resumes from where it left off

Graph has hub nodes with hundreds of edges

This almost always means the schema is too open or entity resolution is not running.

Checklist:

  • Blueprint has closed: true in the ontology section
  • All patterns are specific [SourceType, REL, TargetType] triples
  • Run forge conflicts to see which entities have the most disagreements

docs.title: Serving and answers
docs.text:
lattice-serve starts but agent ask returns no results

Check that both are using the same store: - forge cook --store neo4j writes to Neo4j → start serve with --store neo4j - forge cook --store memory data is gone when the command exited → re-cook with --store neo4j

agent ask refuses to answer

This is intentional. refuse_outside_corpus: true in your blueprint means the agent says "I cannot find that in the documents" rather than guessing from general knowledge.

If the answer should be there:

  1. Check the source was extracted: forge status src-abc123
  2. Re-run extraction: forge cook src-abc123
  3. Rephrase using terms from the document

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
Open an issue at github.com/Kamaal404/RAGmen/issues with:

  • The exact command you ran
  • The full output / error message
  • What you expected to happen

docs.title: Blueprint — Overview
docs.text: A blueprint is the design document that tells RAGmen what to look for in your corpus. It is the most important decision you make in the whole process — and the cheapest, because it happens before any AI cost is spent.

docs.title: What a blueprint defines
docs.text:
mindmap
  root((blueprint.yaml))
    structure
      Heading patterns
      Skip regions
    ontology
      Node types
      Relationship types
      Allowed patterns
    guardrails
      Conflict policy
      Hard filters
      Answer policy
    embedding
      Dimensions
      Targets
Section What it controls structure How to split your document into chunks (headings, skip regions) ontology What kinds of things and relationships exist in your documents guardrails How the serve layer filters and presents answers embedding Vector dimensions and which fields to embed

docs.title: Why you design before you extract
docs.text:
Do not skip this step

Extraction calls the AI on every chunk of your document. A 300-page book with 150 chunks at typical pricing costs $3–15 depending on chunk size and model.

If your schema is wrong — too broad, missing a node type, using the wrong relationship — you discover this when asking questions. Fixing the schema means re-running extraction from scratch.

The blueprint is the cheap part. Get it right first.

The design workflow is:

1. Inspect your corpus (free, offline)
2. List the ten questions your users need answered
3. Design the schema to answer those questions
4. Validate the blueprint (free, offline)
5. Approve and sign
6. Run extraction

Steps 1–5 cost nothing.

docs.title: The one invariant
docs.text:
From AGENTS.md

Forge and Serve make no ontology decisions. They read a validated blueprint and execute it. If either needs to decide what something means, the blueprint is incomplete; fix the blueprint or the spec, never patch around it in Forge.

Corollary: no domain-specific branching in Forge or Serve code. If you are about to write if corpus == "legal", the spec needs a new field instead.

This means your blueprint is the single source of truth. Every extracted entity, every relationship, every guardrail comes from it — nothing is hardcoded in the engine.

docs.title: Closed vs open schema
docs.text:
RAGmen requires a closed schema: the AI is only allowed to create entities and relationships that are declared in the blueprint.

Closed schema (closed: true)

The AI picks from your declared list. Output is predictable, consistent, and searchable.

ontology:
  closed: true
  node_types: [Procedure, Material, Technique, Hazard]

Open schema (avoid)

The AI invents labels freely: "FireStructure", "BuildingTechnique", "WoodType", "DriedGrass"... You end up with thousands of inconsistent labels that poison every search.

docs.title: Blueprint lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft: inspect corpus
    Draft --> Valid: validate passes
    Valid --> Draft: fix errors
    Valid --> Approved: human sign-off
    Approved --> Active: forge add
    Active --> Revised: schema change needed
    Revised --> Valid: validate passes
    Revised --> Active: targeted re-extraction

Once a blueprint is approved and active, you never need to start from scratch if you revise it. Forge re-extracts only the chunks that were processed under the old blueprint hash.

docs.title: Blueprint Reference Example
docs.text:
The firecraft blueprint is the reference implementation that ships with RAGmen. Every feature of the spec is exercised here. Read it alongside this walkthrough.

File: spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml

docs.title: Header
docs.text:
blueprint_version: 1.0.0
blueprint_hash: sha256:b0654b60ba440c9440a286e0df08416a2dec2194db4705e6737f36da45568187
name: firecraft
description: Practical instructional books on fire building, bushcraft and survival.

blueprint_hash is computed automatically by the validator and stamped on every extracted chunk. If you change the blueprint, chunks extracted under the old hash are targeted for re-extraction.

docs.title: Design note
docs.text:
design_note: |
  Procedure is the central node because every declared question is ultimately
  "what do I build / do". Technique is separate from Procedure because ignition
  methods recombine freely across structures: a bow drill lights a teepee or a
  log cabin, and merging them would force a combinatorial explosion of types.
  ...

The design_note is not processed by the system — it is for humans. Write down why you made each design decision. You will thank yourself when revisiting the schema months later.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
structure:
  hierarchy:
    - level: chapter
      pattern: '^\s*(?:CHAPTER|Chapter)\s+([IVXLCDM]+|\d+)\s*[-–—:.]?\s*(.*)$'
      example: "CHAPTER 4 - Tinder and Kindling"
    - level: section
      pattern: '^([A-Z][A-Z0-9''\-]{2,}(?:\s+[A-Z0-9''\-&]+){0,6})\s*$'
      example: "THE DAKOTA FIRE HOLE"
  chunk_at: section
  max_chunk_chars: 5000
  skip_regions:
    - match: '^\s*(CONTENTS|INDEX|ACKNOWLEDGMENTS|ABOUT THE AUTHOR|BIBLIOGRAPHY)'
      span: to_next_heading
      reason: Matches heading patterns and costs tokens to extract nothing.

hierarchy — the two-level structure of this book: chapters contain sections. Each level has: - pattern — a regex that matches headings at that level (Python flavor) - example — a sample heading from the document, for documentation

chunk_at: section — chunks are created at section boundaries. A section is one chunk. This preserves relationships that span multiple paragraphs within a section.

max_chunk_chars: 5000 — sections longer than this are split at subsplit_pattern (step boundaries in this book).

skip_regions — patterns that identify sections to skip entirely before chunking. These would match heading patterns and cost real money to extract nothing useful.

docs.title: Node types
docs.text:
The firecraft blueprint has 8 node types:

Label What it represents Central question Procedure Fire structures (teepee, log cabin, dakota hole) What should I build? Technique Ignition methods (bow drill, ferro rod) How do I light it? Material Things burned (birch bark, dry grass, hardwood) What do I burn? Tool Equipment not consumed (knife, axe, lens) What kit do I need? Purpose Goals (warmth, cooking, signaling) Which fire suits my goal? Condition Environmental circumstances (rain, wind, wet wood) What works in my situation? Hazard Specific dangers (carbon monoxide, ember scatter) What could go wrong? SafetyRule Explicit safety instructions How do I avoid that?

Why Technique is separate from Procedure

A bow drill can light a teepee or a log cabin. Merging them would create a combinatorial explosion: "bow drill teepee", "bow drill log cabin", etc. Keeping them separate lets one technique connect to many procedures.

Why Material has a role property instead of three types

Birch bark can be tinder when shaved thin, or fuel when used in a log. The same material changes role by context. A role property captures this without creating three separate types.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
relationship_types:
  - label: REQUIRES_MATERIAL
    description: This procedure consumes this material at the given stage.
    properties:
      - {name: stage, type: STRING, enum: [tinder, kindling, fuel]}

  - label: SUITED_FOR
    description: Explicitly recommended by the text under this condition.

  - label: UNSUITED_FOR
    description: Explicitly warned against by the text under this condition.

SUITED_FOR and UNSUITED_FOR are separate, not one edge with a flag

The negative case is what a survival reader most needs. A boolean property (suited: false) is exactly what a graph traversal forgets to check. Two separate relationship types make the negative case a first-class citizen.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
patterns:
  - [Procedure, SERVES_PURPOSE, Purpose]
  - [Procedure, REQUIRES_MATERIAL, Material]
  - [Procedure, HAS_HAZARD, Hazard]
  - [Technique, IGNITES, Material]
  - [Technique, REQUIRES_TOOL, Tool]
  - [Hazard, MITIGATED_BY, SafetyRule]
  # ... 18 total

Every allowed connection is declared explicitly. The AI cannot create an edge like [Material, HAS_HAZARD, Procedure] because it is not in the pattern list. This is what prevents hallucinated connections.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
guardrails:
  conflict_policy: prefer_strictest
  hard_filters:
    - name: hazards_always
      mode: force_include
      labels: [Hazard, SafetyRule]
      rationale: A method returned without its warning is worse than no answer.
    - name: source_visibility
      mode: restrict
      params: [user_id]
      cypher: "node.visibility = 'public' OR node.owner_id = $user_id"
      rationale: User-uploaded books are licensed to that user only.
  answer_policy:
    require_citation: true
    refuse_outside_corpus: true

prefer_strictest — when sources conflict on a safety question, the more cautious answer wins.

hazards_always — Hazard and SafetyRule nodes are always included in answers, regardless of the query. This is enforced in Cypher, not the system prompt — it cannot be overridden.

source_visibility — a row-level filter that prevents users from accessing sources they do not own. Enforced as a Cypher WHERE clause.

docs.title: Drift thresholds
docs.text:
drift:
  max_unmapped_mention_rate: 0.15
  max_vocabulary_miss_rate: 0.10
  max_degree: 200
  min_provenance_coverage: 0.85

After each extraction run, forge cook reports a drift summary:

Metric What it measures Threshold unmapped_mention_rate Fraction of entity mentions the AI flagged as outside the schema 15% vocabulary_miss_rate Fraction of Material entities that fell through to LLM resolution 10% max_degree Maximum number of edges on any single node (hub detection) 200 provenance_coverage Fraction of edges that have a source quote 85%

If any threshold is exceeded, the drift report recommends which schema change would fix it — new vocabulary entries, revised patterns, or a new node type.

docs.title: Full file
docs.text:
The complete firecraft.blueprint.yaml is at spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml in the repo. Use it as the starting point for your own blueprint by copying and modifying it.

Command reference

docs.title: Designing a Schema
docs.text: This guide walks through the five steps of designing a blueprint schema for a new corpus.

docs.title: Step 1 — Inspect your corpus
docs.text:
Before writing any YAML, run the inspector on your documents:

python blueprint/scripts/inspect_corpus.py --input your-document.pdf --show-sample

Read the output carefully. It shows you:

  • Heading structure — which regex patterns would match your document's headings
  • Sample text — representative paragraphs from different sections
  • Estimated chunk sizes — how many chunks the document would produce

Tip

Always open the extracted .txt file after inspection. If headings did not survive the PDF extraction, that is a cleanup problem — no amount of schema design will fix it. Re-run with a different PDF engine (--engine pdfplumber).

docs.title: Step 2 — List your workload questions
docs.text:
Write down the ten questions your users most need answered. Be specific:

Generic Specific "Tell me about fires" "Which fire structures require birch bark?" "What are the hazards?" "Which procedures carry a carbon monoxide risk?" "Ingredients?" "What tinder materials work in wet conditions?"

For each specific question, ask yourself: - What types of things appear in this answer? → those become node_types - What connects them? → those become relationship_types

docs.title: Step 3 — Design your node types
docs.text:
Node types are the categories of things in your documents. Start with 3 to 5.

ontology:
  node_types:
    - label: Procedure       # (1)
      description: A fire-building structure or technique
      answers: "What should I build or do?"
      properties:
        - name: name
          type: STRING
          required: true

    - label: Material
      description: A physical material consumed in fire building
      answers: "What do I need?"
      properties:
        - name: name
          type: STRING
          required: true
        - name: role         # (2)
          type: STRING
  1. Labels must be PascalCase with no spaces.
  2. Properties are optional fields the AI extracts per entity. Keep them to 1–2 per type.

Keep it small

A schema with 20 node types is almost always wrong. It produces a hairball where everything is connected to everything and retrieval degrades to random.

Rule of thumb: if you cannot write a one-sentence description for a node type, merge it with another or split it more carefully.

docs.title: Properties: what to extract per entity
docs.text: Use properties for... Avoid properties for... Factual attributes (role, unit, date) Free-text descriptions (just use the chunk text) Hard-filter values (jurisdiction, allergen) Things that would go in another node type

docs.title: Step 4 — Design your relationships
docs.text:
Relationship types connect node types. The key constraint is domain and range — which node types can be source and target.

  relationship_types:
    - label: REQUIRES_MATERIAL
      description: This procedure or technique needs this material

    - label: HAS_HAZARD
      description: This procedure carries this specific hazard

  patterns:              # (1)
    - [Procedure, REQUIRES_MATERIAL, Material]
    - [Technique, REQUIRES_MATERIAL, Material]
    - [Procedure, HAS_HAZARD, Hazard]
  1. Patterns are the closed list of allowed connections. The AI can only create relationships that match one of these exactly. This is what prevents hallucinated edges.

Naming conventions

  • Relationship labels are SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE
  • Name them as verbs or verb phrases: REQUIRES_MATERIAL, HAS_HAZARD, SUPERSEDES, DEFINED_IN
  • Avoid generic names like RELATED_TO or HAS — they tell the retriever nothing

docs.title: Step 5 — Design the structure section
docs.text:
Tell the chunker how your document is organized:

structure:
  hierarchy:
    - level: 1
      label: Chapter
      pattern: '^Chapter\s+\d+'    # (1)
    - level: 2
      label: Section
      pattern: '^\d+\.\d+\s+'
  skip_regions:                    # (2)
    - label: TableOfContents
      start_pattern: '^Table of Contents'
      end_pattern: '^Chapter\s+1'
    - label: Index
      start_pattern: '^Index$'
      end_pattern: null
  1. Patterns are Python regex. Test yours at regex101.com — Python flavor.
  2. Skip regions are ignored during chunking. They would cost tokens to process and produce nothing useful.

Chunk on structural boundaries, not fixed character counts. A legal article is a chunk. A recipe is a chunk. A chapter section is a chunk. Fixed-size splitting cuts relationships in half and those are exactly the relationships you need to extract.

docs.title: Step 6 — Add guardrails
docs.text:
guardrails:
  conflict_policy: surface_both    # (1)
  hard_filters:
    - name: hazards_always
      mode: force_include
      labels: [Hazard]
      rationale: Safety hazards must always surface.
  answer_policy:
    require_citation: true         # (2)
    refuse_outside_corpus: true    # (3)
  1. surface_both — when two sources disagree, show both. last_write_wins picks the most recent.
  2. Every claim in an answer must be backed by a retrievable chunk.
  3. The agent refuses to answer questions it cannot find in the corpus.

Hard filters vs soft filters

Hard filters are enforced in Cypher WHERE clauses — they cannot be overridden by a user prompt. Soft filters are suggestions in the system prompt that the model can ignore.

Anything safety-critical (allergens, hazards, access permissions) should be a hard filter.

docs.title: Step 7 — Validate and approve
docs.text:
python blueprint/scripts/validate_blueprint.py my-blueprint.yaml

Fix any errors reported, then add the approval block:

approved: true
approved_by: your-name
approved_at: "2026-10-12"

Forge will refuse to process documents without an approved blueprint. This is intentional — it forces a conscious sign-off before extraction spend.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake What goes wrong Fix closed: false or missing AI invents thousands of labels Add closed: true Too many node types (>8) Hub nodes, poor retrieval Merge types that answer the same question Patterns too permissive Hallucinated edges everywhere Make every pattern specific: [A, REL, B] No skip_regions Index and TOC entries extracted as entities Add patterns for front matter and indexes Generic relationship names (HAS, RELATED_TO) Retriever cannot distinguish edges Use specific verb phrases

See a complete working example

docs.title: Your First Graph
docs.text: This guide walks you through the complete workflow — from a raw PDF to asking a cited question. We use the example document included with RAGmen (a fire-building manual) so you can follow along immediately.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Make sure you have completed Installation:

  • forge --help works
  • docker compose up -d is running
  • .env file has your API key and Neo4j credentials

docs.title: The workflow at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["① Validate
blueprint"] --> B["② Register
the document"]
    B --> C["③ Dry run
(optional)"]
    C --> D["④ Build
the graph"]
    D --> E["⑤ Start
the server"]
    E --> F["⑥ Ask
a question"]

docs.title: Step 1 — Validate the blueprint
docs.text:
A blueprint is a YAML file that tells RAGmen what to look for in your documents. The repo includes a working blueprint for the fire-building manual:

python blueprint/scripts/validate_blueprint.py spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml

Expected output:

✓ blueprint is valid
  name: firecraft
  version: 1.0.0
  node types: 4 (Procedure, Material, Technique, Hazard)
  patterns: 5

Tip

This step costs nothing — no AI, no database. It just checks that the blueprint file is correctly written. Always do this before adding documents.

docs.title: Step 2 — Register the document
docs.text:
forge add "The Complete Book of Fire Building Campfires for Warmth Light Cooking and Survival.pdf" \
  --blueprint spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml

What happens:

  1. RAGmen reads the PDF and converts it to clean text (fixing headers, footnotes, hyphenation)
  2. The text is split into chunks at chapter and section boundaries
  3. Each chunk gets a unique fingerprint based on its content
  4. Everything is registered in a local database (forge.db)

Expected output:

source registered: src-abc123
mime: application/pdf
chunks: 147
blueprint: firecraft v1.0.0

Note the source ID (src-abc123) — you will use it in the next steps.

Run it a second time on the same file

unchanged, 0 new chunks  (src-abc123)

RAGmen compares the file's fingerprint against the stored one. If nothing changed, it skips everything — zero AI calls, zero cost.

docs.title: Step 3 — Dry run (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
Before spending any API credits, inspect what will be extracted:

forge extract src-abc123 --dry-run

This writes the prompts to a dry-run/ folder. Open one to see exactly what the AI will receive — your blueprint's schema plus a chunk of text.

This is also useful for estimating cost before a large extraction run.

docs.title: Step 4 — Build the graph
docs.text:
Now run the full pipeline:

forge cook src-abc123

This runs five stages in sequence:

Stage What it does Extract Sends each chunk to the AI, extracts entities and relationships per the blueprint schema Resolve Merges duplicate entity names ("bow drill" + "bow-drill" → one node) Embed Converts all entities and chunks to vector representations Write Loads everything into Neo4j Drift report Checks for unmapped mentions, hub violations, pattern violations

Expected output (progress updates as chunks are processed):

[  1/147] Chapter 1 / Introduction ... done
[  2/147] Chapter 1 / Tinder ...       done
...
[147/147] Chapter 12 / Safety ...      done

entities written:   84
relations written: 127
chunks processed:  147
drift: 3 unmapped mentions (see drift report)

If the run is interrupted

Press Ctrl+C to stop at any time, or let a failure happen. Run the same command again:

forge cook src-abc123

It resumes from the last completed chunk. You will never pay twice for the same chunk.

docs.title: Step 5 — Start the retrieval server
docs.text:
Open a second terminal and run:

lattice-serve --store neo4j \
  --blueprint spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml \
  --neo4j-password password

You should see:

Lattice Serve starting (store=neo4j)

Leave this terminal open. The server is now listening for questions.

docs.title: Step 6 — Ask a question
docs.text:
In your first terminal, run:

agent ask "how do I build a dakota fire hole?"

Example response:

The Dakota fire hole is a wind-resistant underground fire structure suited
for cooking and concealment. It consists of two connected holes: the main
fire chamber and a ventilation tunnel that feeds air from the side.

Materials required:
  • dry grass — tinder stage
  • birch bark — kindling stage
  • hardwood — fuel

Hazards:
  ⚠ carbon monoxide risk in enclosed spaces — ensure ventilation

Sources:
  [1] Chapter 2 / Dakota Fire Hole (p. 81)
  [2] Chapter 3 / Ventilation and Safety (p. 94)

Every claim is backed by a source and page number. The agent will not invent information that is not in the document.

docs.title: Things to try
docs.text:
Multi-hop questionConflicting sourcesInspect the graphRemove a source 
agent ask "which fire structures have a carbon monoxide hazard?"

This requires following two relationships in the graph: structure → hazard. Plain search would miss this.

If you add a second document that contradicts the first:

agent ask "what is the best tinder material?"

RAGmen surfaces both answers with attribution:

Source A (manual.pdf, p.12): dry grass is preferred in dry conditions
Source B (guide.pdf, p.7): birch bark is more reliable in wet conditions

forge list                    # all registered sources
forge chunks src-abc123       # chunks for a source
forge status src-abc123       # details and current status
forge conflicts               # multi-source disagreements

forge retract src-abc123

Entities unique to this source are removed. Entities shared with other sources are preserved.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
Ready to use RAGmen on your own documents? The blueprint is the key.

Blueprint design

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Get RAGmen running from scratch in about 10 minutes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Why you need it Minimum version Python RAGmen is written in Python 3.11+ Git To download the code Any recent Docker Desktop Runs the Neo4j knowledge graph database Any recent OpenAI API key Extracts knowledge from your documents —

Can I test without an API key?

Yes. Use --dry-run to inspect what would be extracted, or --provider mock to run a full pipeline with fake extraction data. You only need a real API key when you want actual knowledge extracted.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install Python
docs.text:
Go to python.org/downloads and download Python 3.11 or newer.

WindowsmacOSLinux

During installation, check "Add Python to PATH" — this is easy to miss and causes most installation problems.

Verify it worked by opening Command Prompt or PowerShell and running:

python --version

Install via Homebrew (recommended):

brew install python@3.11

Or download the installer from python.org.

sudo apt install python3.11 python3-pip   # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo dnf install python3.11               # Fedora

You should see something like Python 3.11.9. If you see 3.9 or lower, the wrong version was installed — check again.

docs.title: Step 2 — Install Docker Desktop
docs.text:
Go to docker.com/products/docker-desktop and download Docker Desktop. Install and start it.

Verify it worked:

docker --version

You should see Docker version 27.x.x or similar.

Docker must be running

Docker Desktop must be open and running whenever you use RAGmen. It does not need to be in the foreground, but it must be started.

docs.title: Step 3 — Download RAGmen
docs.text:
Open a terminal and run:

git clone https://github.com/Kamaal404/RAGmen.git
cd RAGmen

docs.title: Step 4 — Install the components
docs.text:
RAGmen has three independently installable components. Install all three:

cd forge && pip install -e ".[dev]" && cd ..
cd serve && pip install -e ".[dev]" && cd ..
cd agent && pip install -e ".[dev]" && cd ..

Verify the main component is installed:

forge --help

You should see a list of forge commands. If you see command not found, the installation did not complete — re-run the pip commands above.

docs.title: Step 5 — Start the database
docs.text:
RAGmen stores the knowledge graph in Neo4j. Start it with:

docker compose up -d

The first run downloads the Neo4j image (~600 MB). After that it starts in a few seconds.

Open http://localhost:7474 in your browser. You should see the Neo4j browser interface. This confirms the database is running.

Default login: neo4j / password

docs.title: Step 6 — Set your credentials
docs.text:
Create a file called .env in the RAGmen folder:

.env
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...your key here...
NEO4J_USER=neo4j
NEO4J_PASSWORD=password

RAGmen reads this file automatically.

Where do I get an OpenAI API key?

Go to platform.openai.com/api-keys, sign in, and create a new key. Keep it secret — treat it like a password.

docs.title: Verify everything works
docs.text:
Run the full test suite — it works completely offline with no API key and no database:

make test

You should see all tests passing with no errors. If any test fails, check the error output and refer to Troubleshooting.

docs.title: What got installed
docs.text:
RAGmen/
├── forge/     ← build-time tool (forge add, forge cook, ...)
├── serve/     ← MCP retrieval server (lattice-serve)
├── agent/     ← answer policy layer (agent ask)
├── spec/      ← blueprint schema and examples
├── blueprint/ ← design-time scripts
└── docs/      ← this documentation

Your First Graph

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
You have documents. A legal archive. A technical handbook. A policy collection. A survival manual. You want to ask questions and get accurate, cited answers.

The simplest approach is to paste everything into an AI and ask. That works for basic questions, but breaks down fast:

What plain AI chat cannot do reliably

  • Multi-hop questions — "Which procedures that require birch bark also have a carbon monoxide hazard?" requires following two relationships across the document.
  • Citations — "Where exactly does it say that?" Plain AI often hallucinates sources.
  • Conflicting sources — If two documents disagree, AI picks one and sounds confident about it.
  • Corpus-only answers — AI mixes in its general training knowledge. You cannot tell which part came from your documents.

RAGmen solves all of these by building a knowledge graph — a structured map of facts and relationships — and answering questions by navigating that map.

docs.title: The cooking metaphor
docs.text:
RAGmen uses a cooking metaphor because building a knowledge graph has the same structure as cooking a meal:

  • Recipe first

    Before you touch your ingredients, you write a recipe. In RAGmen this is the blueprint — a schema that defines what kinds of things and relationships exist in your documents.

    You approve the blueprint before any AI cost is spent.

  • Then cook

    Forge reads your documents, breaks them into structured pieces, sends them to an AI for extraction, resolves duplicates, and writes everything into a knowledge graph.

    Forge runs once per document and resumes automatically if interrupted.

  • Then serve

    Serve is the read-only window into the graph. It combines vector search, keyword search, and graph traversal to find the best answer — then Agent formats it with citations.

docs.title: The three components
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph DESIGN["Blueprint  —  design time, human-gated"]
        B["blueprint.yaml\nWhat to look for\nApproved by you"]
    end

    subgraph BUILD["Forge  —  build time, unattended"]
        F1[Load & chunk] --> F2[Extract] --> F3[Resolve] --> F4[Embed] --> F5[Write]
    end

    subgraph QUERY["Serve + Agent  —  per question, read-only"]
        S[Hybrid search] --> A[Cited answer]
    end

    DESIGN -->|"validated blueprint"| BUILD
    BUILD -->|"graph + vectors"| QUERY

The one invariant

Forge and Serve make no ontology decisions. They read a validated blueprint and execute it. If either needs to decide what something means, the blueprint is incomplete — fix the blueprint, not the code.

docs.title: What makes it different
docs.text: Plain AI chat RAGmen Answers strictly from your documents Every claim has a source + page Multi-hop reasoning across relationships Surfaces conflicting sources Re-adding an unchanged file costs nothing — Interrupted run resumes where it stopped —

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text:
RAGmen is for anyone with a body of documents they need to query reliably:

  • A law firm querying a client's contract archive
  • A fire safety instructor querying a survival manual
  • A policy team querying government regulations
  • A technical writer querying a product manual collection

Do I need to know how to code?

No. You need to be comfortable running commands in a terminal. The guides here walk through every step.

docs.title: agent — Command Reference
docs.text: The Agent is the answer policy layer. It calls Serve's retrieval tools, formats the results, enforces citation requirements, and surfaces conflicting sources.

docs.title: agent ask
docs.text:
Ask a single question.

agent ask "how do I build a dakota fire hole?"
agent ask "which fire structures are suited for cooking?"
agent ask "what tinder works in wet conditions?"

What happens:

  1. Calls serve.search with your query
  2. Expands any high-scoring entities with serve.expand
  3. Verifies each claim with serve.cite
  4. Formats the answer with inline citations
  5. If conflicts exist, surfaces both sides with attribution
  6. If the answer is not in the corpus, refuses to answer

docs.title: agent interactive
docs.text:
Opens a question loop so you can ask multiple questions without restarting.

agent interactive

RAGmen › how do I build a dakota fire hole?
...answer...

RAGmen › what about in wet conditions?
...answer...

RAGmen › quit

docs.title: Answer policies
docs.text:
The agent enforces the policies declared in your blueprint's answer_policy section:

Policy What it does require_citation: true Every factual claim in the answer must be backed by a retrievable chunk. Claims without a source are dropped. refuse_outside_corpus: true If the answer cannot be found in the indexed documents, the agent says so instead of drawing on general AI knowledge.

These are not suggestions — they are structural constraints on how answers are assembled.

docs.title: Conflict surfacing
docs.text:
When conflict_policy: surface_both is set in the blueprint:

Question: what is the best tinder material?

Source A (manual.pdf, p.12):
  Dry grass is the most readily available tinder in temperate climates.
  [Chapter 1 / Tinder]

Source B (guide.pdf, p.7):
  Dry grass fails in wet conditions. Birch bark is more reliable.
  [Chapter 2 / Material Selection]

These sources disagree. Both are shown as recorded.

When conflict_policy: prefer_strictest is set (appropriate for safety-critical corpora), the more cautious assertion is used and the conflict is noted.

docs.title: Citation format
docs.text:
Every answer includes citations in the form:

[1] Chapter 2 / Dakota Fire Hole (manual.pdf, p.81)
[2] Chapter 3 / Ventilation (manual.pdf, p.94)

Each citation number corresponds to a specific chunk. Run serve cite <chunk_id> to retrieve the verbatim text from that chunk.

docs.title: forge — Command Reference
docs.text: Forge is the build-time tool. It registers documents, chunks them, extracts knowledge, and writes the graph. Run forge --help at any time.

docs.title: forge add
docs.text:
Register a document and split it into chunks.

forge add <path> --blueprint <blueprint.yaml> [options]

Arguments:

Argument Required Description <path> Yes Path to the file (PDF, Markdown, TXT, HTML) --blueprint Yes Path to the approved blueprint YAML --owner No Who is adding this source (stored in registry) --visibility No public or private (default: public)

Example:

forge add manual.pdf --blueprint spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml --owner alice

What it does:

  1. Converts the file to clean text (PDF: fixes headers, hyphenation, reflow)
  2. Splits text into chunks at structural boundaries from blueprint.structure
  3. Applies skip_regions to exclude front matter, indexes, etc.
  4. Assigns a content-addressed ID to each chunk: hash(source_id + path + text)
  5. Registers the source and chunks in forge.db

Idempotent by design

Running forge add on an unchanged file outputs:

unchanged, 0 new chunks  (src-abc123)

RAGmen compares the file's SHA-256 fingerprint and skips everything if nothing changed. Zero AI calls, zero cost.

docs.title: forge list
docs.text:
Show all registered sources.

forge list
forge list --status ready

Status values:

Value Meaning chunking Being processed ready Chunked, waiting for extraction extracted Extraction complete retracted Removed

docs.title: forge status
docs.text:
Show details for one source.

forge status src-abc123

Output includes: file path, content hash, chunk count, blueprint used, current status, added by, added at.

docs.title: forge chunks
docs.text:
Show the chunks for a source.

forge chunks src-abc123
forge chunks src-abc123 --json

Each chunk shows its breadcrumb path in the document hierarchy, page number, character range, and text preview.

docs.title: forge extract
docs.text:
Run extraction on a registered source. Sends chunks to the AI and extracts entities + relationships per the blueprint schema.

forge extract src-abc123
forge extract src-abc123 --dry-run
forge extract src-abc123 --provider mock

Options:

Option Description --dry-run Write prompts to disk without calling the AI --dry-run-dir <dir> Where to write dry-run output (default: dry-run/) --provider mock Use a mock provider that returns fake data (no API key needed) --provider openai Use OpenAI (default)

Always dry-run first on a new blueprint

The dry-run shows exactly what the AI will receive — your schema plus a chunk of text. Check that the schema looks right before spending on a full extraction run.

docs.title: forge cook
docs.text:
Run the complete pipeline: extract → resolve → embed → write to graph.

forge cook src-abc123
forge cook src-abc123 --store neo4j
forge cook src-abc123 --store memory

Options:

Option Description Default --store neo4j Write to the running Neo4j instance neo4j --store memory Write to an in-process dict (lost when command exits) —

Stages:

extract   → AI reads chunks, outputs typed entities and relationships
resolve   → Deduplication: "bow drill" + "bow-drill" → one node
embed     → Vectors computed for all entities and chunks
write     → Everything loaded into the graph store
report    → Drift: unmapped mentions, hub violations, coverage

Kill-safe by design

Every chunk has a per-chunk status in the job ledger. If forge cook is interrupted — by Ctrl+C, a crash, or a power cut — run the same command again. It resumes from the last completed chunk. You will never pay twice for the same chunk.

docs.title: forge update
docs.text:
Re-run extraction on a source where the file has changed.

forge update src-abc123

Forge compares the new version against the stored chunks. Only changed chunks are re-extracted. Unchanged chunks are skipped.

docs.title: forge retract
docs.text:
Remove a source and all its data from the graph.

forge retract src-abc123

What gets removed:

  • All chunks for this source
  • All entities that are only referenced by this source
  • Embeddings for removed entities and chunks

What is preserved:

  • Entities shared with other sources (refcounting protects them)
  • All data from other sources

This is safe to run at any time without affecting other sources.

docs.title: forge conflicts
docs.text:
List cases where two or more sources make contradictory assertions.

forge conflicts

Example output:

CONFLICT: Procedure "bow drill" — REQUIRES_MATERIAL — Material "dry grass"
  Asserted by: src-abc123 (manual.pdf p.12): "dry grass is preferred"
  Asserted by: src-def456 (guide.pdf  p.7):  "dry grass does not work in wet conditions"

1 conflict found

Conflicts are surfaced in answers automatically when conflict_policy: surface_both is set in the blueprint.

docs.title: forge blueprint
docs.text:
Validate a blueprint file without adding any sources.

forge blueprint my-blueprint.yaml
forge blueprint my-blueprint.yaml --check

Equivalent to running python blueprint/scripts/validate_blueprint.py directly.

docs.title: lattice-serve — Command Reference
docs.text: Lattice Serve is the read-only MCP retrieval server. It never writes to the graph. Start it once and leave it running while users ask questions.

docs.title: Starting the server
docs.text:
lattice-serve --store neo4j --blueprint spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml

For development and testing (in-memory, data lost on exit):

lattice-serve --store memory --blueprint spec/examples/firecraft.blueprint.yaml

Options:

Option Description Default --store neo4j or memory memory --blueprint Blueprint YAML to load guardrails from (none) --neo4j-uri Neo4j Bolt URI bolt://localhost:7687 --neo4j-user Neo4j username neo4j --neo4j-password Neo4j password (empty)

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text: Serve exposes five tools over the Model Context Protocol. These are called automatically by agent ask, or you can call them directly from any MCP client.

docs.title: search
docs.text:
Hybrid retrieval: combines vector similarity, keyword match, and graph traversal using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

{
  "query": "how do I start a fire in wet conditions",
  "top_k": 10,
  "hops": 1
}
Parameter Description Default query Natural language query — top_k Number of results to return 10 hops Graph traversal depth after initial hits 1

How it works:

flowchart LR
    Q["query"] --> V["Vector search\n(cosine similarity)"]
    Q --> K["Keyword search\n(fulltext index)"]
    V --> R["RRF fusion\n(reranking)"]
    K --> R
    R --> G["Graph expansion\n(k hops)"]
    G --> F["Guardrail filters\n(Cypher WHERE)"]
    F --> Out["Ranked results\n+ citations"]

The guardrails from your blueprint are applied as Cypher WHERE clauses before results are returned. Hard filters (like hazards_always) cannot be overridden.

docs.title: expand
docs.text:
Explore the neighbourhood of a chunk or entity.

{
  "node_id": "chunk001",
  "hops": 2,
  "top_k": 20
}
Parameter Description Default node_id Chunk ID or entity ID — hops Traversal depth 1 top_k Maximum results 20

Use this when you already know a relevant chunk or entity and want to see what is nearby in the graph.

docs.title: cite
docs.text:
Get the verbatim text, source URI, and page number for a chunk.

{
  "chunk_id": "chunk001"
}

Returns:

Chunk: chunk001
Path: Chapter 2 / Dakota Fire Hole
Source: manual.pdf
Page: 81
Characters: [4200, 4800)
Blueprint: sha256:b0654b60...

The Dakota fire hole is a wind-resistant underground structure...

Every claim in an agent ask answer is backed by a cite call. The citation includes the exact character range so the source can be verified precisely.

docs.title: explain_path
docs.text:
Show how two entities are connected in the graph.

{
  "source_label": "Procedure",
  "source_name": "dakota fire hole",
  "target_label": "Hazard",
  "target_name": "carbon monoxide",
  "max_depth": 4
}

Returns the chain of relationships connecting the two entities:

Path found:
  [0] Procedure : dakota fire hole  (start)
  [1] Hazard : carbon monoxide
       └─ HAS_HAZARD  "carbon monoxide is a risk in enclosed spaces"

docs.title: schema
docs.text:
Return the active blueprint ontology.

{}

Returns the full ontology from the loaded blueprint — node types, relationship types, allowed patterns. Useful for understanding what the graph contains before querying.

docs.title: How guardrails are applied
docs.text:
Guardrails from the blueprint are compiled to Cypher WHERE clauses before any query runs. They are enforced at the database level and cannot be overridden by a user prompt.

Guardrail type How it is enforced force_include Result set is expanded to always include matching nodes restrict WHERE clause filters nodes the user is not permitted to see answer_policy Passed to the Agent layer as enforced constraints

This means a safety hazard that is a force_include guardrail will appear in every answer that touches its parent entity — even if the user's question did not ask about hazards.
